Hebrew Bible ==== Shiloh is mentioned in the Books of [[Book of Genesis| Genesis]], [[Book of Joshua|Joshua]], [[Book of Judges|Judges]], [[1 Samuel]], [[1 Kings]], [[Psalms]], and [[Book of Jeremiah|Jeremiah]]. Shiloh was first mentioned in the Hebrew Bible in the [[Blessing of Jacob]] in Genesis 49:10:
The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet until '''Shiloh''' come; and unto Him shall the gathering of the people be.{{cite web |title=Genesis 49:10 (21st Century King James Version) |website=[[Bible Gateway]] |url= https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis%2049&version=KJ21 }}
In the Book of Joshua, when the Israelites arrived in the land, they set up the Tabernacle. There Joshua and [[Eleazar]] divided the land among the [[Twelve Tribes of Israel|Twelve Tribes]] who had not yet received their allocation in [[Joshua 18#Verses 1–10 |Joshua 18:1–10]], and dealt with the allocation of [[Levitical city|Levitical cities]] in [[Joshua 21]]:1–8. Subsequently, Shiloh became one of the leading religious shrines in ancient Israel, a status it held until shortly before [[David]]'s elevation of [[Jerusalem]].{{cite book |first1=LaMar C. |last1=Berrett |first2=D. Kelly |last2=Ogden |title=Discovering The World of The Bible |publisher=Grandin Book |date=1996 |isbn=0-910523-52-5 |page=94 }} Cf. Also {{harvnb|Schley|1989|pp=191ff}} Joshua 18:1 notes, "The whole congregation of Israel assembled together at Shiloh and set up the tent (or tabernacle) of the congregation there." The tabernacle had been built under [[Moses]]' direction from God in [[Book of Exodus |Exodus]] 26 (discussed in the ''[[parashah]]'' [[Terumah (parashah)#readings| "Terumah"]]) to house the [[Ark of the Covenant]], also made according to Moses' instructions from God in [[Exodus 25]]. [[Talmud]]ic sources state that the Tabernacle remained at Shiloh for 369 years,{{cite web|url=http://www.mechon-mamre.org/b/l/l5114.htm |title=Zevachim 118B |publisher=Mechon Mamre |access-date=2013-08-17}} until the Ark of the Covenant was taken into the battle camp at [[Eben-Ezer]] in [[1 Samuel 4]]:3–5 and captured by the [[Philistines]] at [[Aphek (biblical) |Aphek]] (probably [[Antipatris]]). At some point during its long stay at Shiloh, the portable tent seems to have been enclosed within a holy compound—in Greek, a "[[temenos]]". It was at Shiloh that [[Eli (biblical figure)|Eli]] and [[Samuel]] ministered according to [[1 Samuel]] ({{bibleref|1|Sam|3:21}}). At some point, the Tabernacle was moved to [[Gibeon (ancient city)|Gibeon]] according to [[1 Chronicles 16]] and [[1 Chronicles 21|21]], and [[2 Chronicles 1]] ({{bibleref|1|Chr|16:39–40}}, {{bibleref|1|Chr|21:20}}, {{bibleref|2|Chr|1:39–2}}), which became an Israelite holy site under David and [[Solomon]]. The people made [[pilgrimage]]s there for major feasts and sacrifices, and [[Judges 21]] records the place as the site of an annual dance of maidens among the [[vineyard]]s. [[File:Location_and_remains_of_the_Tabernacle_IMG_2982.JPG|thumb|Presumed location of the Tabernacle at Shiloh]] According to [[1 Samuel 1]]–[[1 Samuel 3|3]], the sanctuary at Shiloh was administered by [[Eli (Judges)|Eli]], the [[High Priest of Israel|High Priest]], and his two sons [[Hophni and Phinehas]]. According to this account, the young Samuel was dedicated by his mother [[Hannah (biblical figure) |Hannah]] there, to be raised at the shrine by the high priest, and his own prophetic ministry is presented as having begun there. It was under Eli and his sons that the Ark was lost to Israel in a battle with the Philistines at [[Aphek (biblical)|Aphek]]. [[W.F. Albright]] hypothesized that the Philistines also destroyed Shiloh at this time; this conclusion is disputed,{{harvnb|Schley|1989|pp=184–199}} but supported by recent archaeological research.[https://www.huffingtonpost.com/2013/01/15/tel-shiloh-archaeological-dig-pitcher-city-israel-burned_n_2479718.html Bennett-Smith, Meredith. "Tel Shiloh Archaeological Dig Pitcher Suggests Biblical City In Israel Burned To Ground"], ''Huffington Post'', January 15, 2013.{{rp|238}} The place may have been destroyed later as well, though the biblical text records no such claimed destruction. Certainly, the shadowy figure of [[Prophets in Judaism |prophet]] [[Ahijah the Shilonite]],{{cite web |url=http://www.mechon-mamre.org/e/et/et09a14.htm |title=1 Kings 14:6–16 |publisher=Mechon-mamre |access-date=2013-08-17}} who instigated the revolt of [[Jeroboam I]] against David's grandson [[Rehoboam]] in [[1 Kings 11]] and [[1 Kings 14|14]], came from there and he bore the same name as the Aaronite priest that consulted the Ark for Saul in [[1 Samuel 14]]:3. Schley has claimed that the capture of the Ark and the death of Saul occurred in the same battle and that the later Davidic editors redacted the texts to make it appear as if Saul had ruled without either Tent Shrine or Ark, and thus without sacral legitimacy.{{harvnb|Schley|1989|pp=191–7}} What is certain is that during the prophetic ministry of [[Jeremiah]] in [[Jeremiah 7]]:12–15; [[Jeremiah 26|26]]:5–9, and [[Jeremiah 41|41]]:5 over three hundred years later, Shiloh had been reduced to ruins. Jeremiah used the example of Shiloh to warn the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem what God would do to the "place where I caused my name to dwell", warning them that their holy city, Jerusalem, like Shiloh, could fall under divine judgment.{{rp|240}} According to [[Richard Elliott Friedman]], the priesthood of Shiloh was the [[Elohist]] source of the [[documentary hypothesis]] and also provided much of the material of the [[Deuteronomistic history]], with the writer of this history (Jeremiah or somebody closely connected to him) being a descendant of these priests. If correct, this would make Shiloh a major source of the history part of the Hebrew Bible/Old Testament.{{rp|231-232}} === Hellenistic and Roman periods === According to historical records, the area's population was diverse on the eve of the [[Maccabean Revolt]] in 167 BCE. During the revolt, clashes erupted between the numerous ethnic groups in the vicinity. Several accounts suggest the presence of [[Edom]]ites in the region; [[Jews|Jewish]] communities are also implied. Like in western Samaria, it's possible that [[Seleucid Empire|Seleucid]] veterans settled here as well. Archeological evidence indicates that Shiloh, then a gentile settlement, was violently destroyed in the mid 2nd century BCE. It was suggested that this destruction might be connected to the conquests of [[Hasmonean dynasty|Hasmonean]] leaders [[Jonathan Apphus]] and [[Simon Thassi]].{{Cite journal |last=לויתן־בן אריה |first=רעות |date=2021 |title=שכבת חורבן מהתקופה ההלניסטית בתל שילה |trans-title=A Destruction Layer from the Hellenistic Period at Tel Shiloh |url=https://www.ariel.ac.il/wp/ihd/2021/05/18/%d7%a9%d7%9b%d7%91%d7%aa-%d7%97%d7%95%d7%a8%d7%91%d7%9f-%d7%9e%d7%94%d7%aa%d7%a7%d7%95%d7%a4%d7%94-%d7%94%d7%94%d7%9c%d7%a0%d7%99%d7%a1%d7%98%d7%99%d7%aa-%d7%91%d7%aa%d7%9c-%d7%a9%d7%99%d7%9c%d7%94/ |journal=במעבה ההר |language=Hebrew |volume=11 |issue=1 |pages=53–71}} ===Byzantine period=== [[File:Shilo, Palestine (13056127775).jpg|250px|thumbnail|The Byzantine basilica, with excavations to the right.]] [[Jerome]], in his letter to [[Paula of Rome|Paula]] and [[Eustochium]], dated about 392–393 CE, writes: "With Christ at our side we shall pass through Shiloh and Bethel " (Ep.46,13, PL 22, 492). The official church of Jerusalem did not schedule an annual pilgrimage to Shiloh, unlike Bethel. On the contrary, Samuel's feast was held on August 20 in the village of Masephta ([[Mizpah in Benjamin|Mizpah]]). Even the pilgrims seemingly did not visit Shiloh, for the only one that mentions its name—the sixth-century pilgrim Theodosius in ''[[De situ terrae sanctae]]'' (ch. 4, CCSL 175, 116)—wrongly locates it midway between Jerusalem and [[Emmaus Nicopolis]]. The mistaken identification persisted for centuries, as evident, for example, on the Florentine map of 1300, which places Shiloh at [[Nabi Samwil]], where the [[Tomb of Samuel]] is located. The sixth-century mosaic [[Madaba Map]] wrongly locates Shiloh east of [[Shechem]], omitting the depiction of the church. ===Early Muslim and Crusader periods=== In 638, the [[Muslim conquest of the Levant|Muslims conquered Palestine]]. Muslim pilgrims to Shiloh mention a [[mosque]] called ''al-Sakina'', where the memory of Jacob's and Joseph's deeds was revered.{{clarification needed|reason=The deeds are not stated in the article|date=August 2026}} The earliest source is al-Harawi, who visited it in 1173 when it was part of the [[Crusader state]] of the [[Kingdom of Jerusalem]], and wrote, "Seilun is the village of the mosque es-Sekineh where the stone of the Table is found". Yaqut (1225) and el-Quarwini (1308, Marmardji, 94–95), write similarly. ==Archaeology== {{further information|Shilo (Israeli settlement)#Tel Shilo}} ===Overview=== Archaeological excavations have shown that the place was already settled from about 1750 BCE (Middle Bronze II or MB II, otherwise known as MB IIB according to the Albright school); however, it is not mentioned in any pre-biblical source. A tell and many impressive remains have been unearthed from the [[Canaan]]ite and [[Israelite]] eras, with habitation lasting until the 8th century BCE. During the following 12 centuries Shiloh is solely noted as a station on sojourners' routes, usually having only its religious-historical significance to offer. Archaeological excavations have revealed remains from the Roman and Persian as well as Early and Late Muslim periods. An impressive [[glacis]] has been located and pottery, animal remains, weapons and other objects have been recovered.{{dubious|this last sentence MAKES NO SENSE here if not connected to a historical period! The glacis: is it the one mentioned below, from Middle Bronze III? What about the pottery, animal bones, weapons?|date=June 2016}}[[File:Tel_Shiloh_(biblical_site)_2017.jpg|thumb|Tel Shiloh visible in the foreground]] ===History of excavations=== Soundings were first made in 1922 by Aage Schmidt.{{Cite journal |last=Albright |first=W. F. |date=1923 |title=The Danish Excavations at Shiloh |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.2307/1355044 |journal=Bulletin of the American Schools of Oriental Research |language=en |volume=9 |pages=10–11 |doi=10.2307/1355044 |issn=}} A Danish team led by Hans Kjær (overseen by W.F. Albright) excavated between the years 1926 and 1932.{{Cite web |last= |date=2014-01-11 |title=Tel Shiloh (Khirbet Seilun) |url=https://emekshaveh.org/en/tel-shiloh-khirbet-seilun/ |access-date=2026-07-04 |website=[[Emek Shaveh]] |language=en}} A probe was done by Sven Holm-Nielson and Marie-Louise Buhl in 1963. An extensive excavation was done by [[Israel Finkelstein]] during the years 1981–84. Since 2006 further excavations have taken place there. Digs are currently run by Scott Stripling.{{citation needed|date=July 2022}} Under international law an occupying power is not permitted to carry out archaeological excavations except to preserve or rescue a site.{{citation |last=Stahl |first=Ziv |title=Appropriating the Past Israel's Archaeological Practices in the West Bank |publisher=[[Emek Shaveh]] |url=https://emekshaveh.org/en/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/Menachsim-Eng-Web.pdf |pages=5-6, 24}} ===Finkelstein excavations=== Finkelstein's work established eight strata, ranging from Middle Bronze II to the [[Byzantine Empire|Byzantine]] period. [[File:Ancient_Shiloh_IMG_2874.JPG|thumb|Map of the present-day archaeological site]] ====Bronze Age==== A massive wall is attributed to the Middle Bronze III (MB IIC) stage, preserved at a height of {{convert|24|ft|m|order=flip}} and width up to {{convert|18|ft|m|order=flip}}, with an extensive [[glacis]]. ====Iron Age==== The [[Iron Age|Iron]] I (Israelite) remains yielded a pillared two-storey public building near the top of the tell, the earliest attributed to Israelites. Collared rim storage jars and some cultic items were found in these buildings, pointing to usage as part of a cultic complex. More than 20 silos were uncovered from this era, included one with carbonized wheat. The [[destruction layer]] evident throughout the tell may have occurred in the wake of the Philistine victory at [[Eben-Ezer]]. According to [[radiocarbon dating]] by Finkelstein, the site was abandoned [[:he:שילה (עיר מקראית)#cite note-2|around 1050 BCE]], and then sparsely repopulated during the Iron II period. [[Jeremiah]]'s admonition in the course of his temple [[sermon]], "Go now to my place that was in Shiloh" ({{bibleverse|Jeremiah|7:12}}), would have occurred during this era. ====Cultic site==== One of the more intriguing finds was that of a heap of pottery outside the city wall before the advent of the Israelite culture (c. 1000 BCE).{{citation needed|date=September 2015}} This pile of pottery was the remnant of a number of animal sacrifices, which were tossed over the wall after completion of the ritual and then buried. This find points to a sacral status of Shiloh during the Canaanite period, a status adopted by the Israelites. The top of the tell, where Finkelstein supposes that the tabernacle would have been placed, is now exposed bedrock, offering no clues concerning Israelite worship (aside from the adjacent storage complex). ====Roman and Byzantine periods==== More substantive villages emerged in the Roman and Byzantine periods. [[File:By Ovedc Elef-Milim in Tel Shilo 38.jpg|250px|thumbnail|Mosaics under the Jami' al-Yatim]] ===Byzantine churches=== Excavations from 2006 to 2007, carried out adjacent to and just south of Tel Shiloh, exposed elaborate mosaic floors as well as several Greek inscriptions, one explicitly referring to the site as the "village of Shiloh".{{citation needed|date=June 2016}} During August–September 2006 archaeological excavations were carried out adjacent to the tell of Shiloh. A team led by the [[Archaeological Staff Officer of Judea and Samaria|Archaeological Staff Officer]] for [[Judea and Samaria Area]] in [[Israel Antiquities Authority|Israel's Civilian Administration Antiquities Unit]], performing a clean-up operation at Shiloh this summer, a belated continuation to a previous 1998 dig, discovered the [[mosaic]] floor of a large Byzantine church which was probably constructed between 380 and 420. Three Byzantine [[basilica]]s have now been uncovered.{{cite web |url=http://www.christusrex.org/www1/ofm/mad/discussion/034discuss.htm |title=Mount Ephraim and Benjamin: 34. Selo, where the ark stayed - (Kh. Saylun) |last1=Alliata |first1=Eugenio |last2=de Luca |first2=Stefano |work=Christus Rex |access-date=25 December 2015 }}{{dead link|date=May 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} The length of one, excavated by Hans Klær in the late 1920s, is {{convert|40|m|ft}}. The width, also measured externally, is {{convert|14.10|m|ft}}, but a {{convert|6.40|m|ft|adj=on}} wide room adjoins the building on the south side. This church had three naves, and 12 bases and two beautiful [[Corinthian order|Corinthian]] capitals {{convert|62|cm|in|abbr=on}} high and {{convert|72| - |61|cm|in|abbr=on}} wide are preserved. Their appearance recalls the well-known fourth-century style, with separate leaves revealing the ribbing of the back leaves, and a smooth leaf under the corner. A structure discovered in 2006 lies under a Muslim free-standing structure known as [[Mazar (mausoleum)|Weli]] Yetaim. It appears to have experienced problems with water drainage in its western section, despite the installation of runoff pipes and troughs. It appears that the solution was to raise the building's level and lay a new mosaic floor. It was the older, original floor at the lower level that was revealed during the summer of 2006. The [[:he:שילה (עיר מקראית)#cite note-2|mosaic contains geometric designs]], a cross, flora representations and three inscriptions, one, a dedication of a bench, the second, a salute to the residents of ''Siloun'' (as set in mosaic in [[uncial script]]: {{lang|grc|CIλOYN}}) and the third, a general wish for good tidings. Another discovery of an addition to one of the basilicas occurred in 2013.{{cite news |url= http://www.israelhayom.com/site/newsletter_article.php?id=8751 |title= Ancient church discovered at site where Ark of the Covenant once stood |work= [[Israel Hayom]] |access-date= 25 December 2015}} ==Ambiguous use of "Shiloh" in Hebrew Bible== {{Main article|Shiloh (biblical figure)}} [[Shiloh (biblical figure)|Shiloh]] is mentioned in the Hebrew Bible in [[Book of Genesis|Genesis]] as part of the benediction given by [[Jacob]] to his son [[Judah (Bible)|Judah]]: "The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh comes, and unto him shall the gathering of the people be." ({{bibleverse|Genesis|49:10}}). It could be a figure, perhaps the [https://www.christiancourier.com/articles/1101-who-is-the-mysterious-shiloh Messiah], or a place, as mentioned later [https://web.archive.org/web/20131029204541/http://www.biblestudytools.com/judges/passage.aspx?q=judges+21:19-21 in Judges] and also in [http://www.mechon-mamre.org/e/et/et1141.htm Jeremiah 41:5]. ===Messianic Jewish and some Christian interpretations=== [[Messianic Judaism]] became attached to Shiloh as a result of this verse. Shiloh is believed to refer to Jesus by some Christians. {{Short description|Ancient Israelite town in the Gilead, mentioned in the Hebrew Bible}}
'''Jabesh-Gilead''' ({{Langx|he|יָבֵשׁ גִּלְעָד}} ''Yāḇēš Gilʿāḏ''), sometimes shortened to '''Jabesh''', was an ancient [[Israelite]] town in [[Gilead]], in northwest [[Jordan]]. Jabesh is mentioned several times in the [[Hebrew Bible]] primarily in connection with [[King Saul]]'s battles against the [[Ammon]]ites and [[Philistines]].

Jabesh Gilead means Jabesh of Gilead or Jabesh in Gilead, i.e. the town Jabesh in the region of Gilead, as opposed to other towns called Jabesh in other parts of the country.

Jabesh means "dry" in [[Hebrew language|Hebrew]],<ref>{{cite web|title=morfix dictionary|url=http://www.morfix.co.il/%D7%99%D7%91%D7%A9}}</ref> a name possibly attributed to the site's well-draining soil.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=McDonald|first=Burton|url=https://www.bu.edu/asor/pubs/books-monographs/macdonald.pdf|title=East of the Jordan: Territories and Sites of the Hebrew Scriptures|publisher=American Schools of Oriental Research|year=2000|pages=202–203}}</ref> Gilead means 'heap [of stones] of testimony'. There is also an alternative theory that it means 'rocky region'. [Smith's Bible Dictionary, "Gil'e-ad"].

==History==

=== In the Hebrew Bible ===
Jabesh-Gilead is mentioned in the [[Book of Judges]],<ref>{{cite web|title=Judges 21:8-15 (Bible)|url=http://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Judges%2021:%208-15&version=9;|publisher=Bible Gateway|access-date=2007-12-08}}</ref> 
in the first<ref>{{cite web|title=1 Samuel 11:1-11 (Bible)|url=http://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=1%20Samuel%2011:%201-11;&version=49;|publisher=Bible Gateway|access-date=2007-12-08}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=1 Samuel 31:11-13 (Bible)|url=http://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=1%20Samuel%2031:%2011-13&version=9;;|publisher=Bible Gateway|access-date=2007-12-08}}</ref> and second<ref>{{cite web|title=2 Samuel 2:4-5 (Bible)|url=http://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=2%20Samuel%202:%204,5&version=9;|publisher=Bible Gateway|access-date=2007-12-08}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=2 Samuel 21:12 (Bible)|url=http://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=2%20Samuel%2021:%2012&version=9;|publisher=Bible Gateway|access-date=2007-12-08}}</ref> [[Books of Samuel]], and in the [[Book of Chronicles]].<ref>{{cite web|title=1 Chronicles 10:11-12 (Bible)|url=http://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=1%20Chronicles%2010:%2011,12&version=9;|publisher=Bible Gateway|access-date=2007-12-08}}</ref>

==== Benjaminite War ====

Jabesh is mentioned in the biblical episode of the [[Levite's concubine]], also known as the Benjamite War,{{Citation needed|date=July 2026}} during which eleven tribes of Israel had massacred the [[Tribe of Benjamin]]. The eleven tribes relented from wiping out the whole tribe, and decided that they needed to find wives for the 600 remaining Benjaminite men since all other people in Benjamin had been killed. However, they had taken an oath not to give their daughters to a Benjaminite, so they found the one city in Israel that had not joined the fight: Jabesh. The city's inhabitants were executed under the [[Herem (war or property)|Herem]] except for 400 virgins. They brought back 400 virgins from Jabesh and gave them to the men on Rimmon Rock ({{Bibleverse|Judges|21:8-15}}).[[File:067.The_Benjaminites_Take_the_Virgins_of_Jabesh-gilead.jpg|thumb|The Benjaminites take the virgins of Jabesh-gilead, drawing by [[Gustave Doré]]]]

==== Nahash of Ammon ====
Jabesh-Gilead is a central setting of {{Bibleverse|1 Samuel|11}}. After [[Saul]] is [[Anointing|anointed]] by [[Samuel]], [[Nahash of Ammon]] attacks Jabesh-Gilead. Having subjected the town to a [[siege]], its inhabitants sought terms for [[Surrender (military)|surrender]], but were told by Nahash that they had a choice of death by sword or having their right eyes gouged out. The population obtained seven days' grace from Nahash, during which they would be allowed to seek help from the Israelites, after which they would have to submit to the terms of surrender. The town's inhabitants sought help from the people of Israel, sending messengers throughout the whole territory, and [[Saul]] responded by raising an army which decisively defeated Nahash and his cohorts at [[Adoni-Bezek#Bezek|Bezek]]. After the war is over, the Israelites assemble at [[Gilgal]] to renew Saul's kingship over [[Kingdom of Israel (united monarchy)|Israel]].

==== Saul's death ====

After Saul [[Suicide methods|falls on his sword]] during the [[Battle of Gilboa]], the victorious Philistines recover his body as well as those of his three sons who also died in the battle, decapitate them and display them on the wall of [[Beit She'an]]. At night, the inhabitants of Jabesh-Gilead retrieve the bodies, showing their devotion to the rescuer of the city. Following a funeral pyre, the bones of Saul and his sons were buried under the [[Tamarix|tamarisk]] tree in Jabesh ({{Bibleverse|1 Samuel|31:8-13|9}}, {{Bibleverse|1 Chronicles|10:12|9}}). When David learns it was the men of Jabesh-Gilead who had brought Saul to an honorable burial, he sent messengers to bless them "And David sent messengers to the men of Yavesh-Gilad, and said to them: ‘May you be blessed of Hashem, that you have shown this kindness to your lord, to Saul, and buried him.’”({{Bibleverse|2 Samuel|2:4-7|9}}). Later, David takes the bones of Saul and of his son Jonathan from Jabesh and buries them in [[Zelah, Judea|Zela]], in the tomb of [[Kish (Bible)|Saul's father]] ({{Bibleverse|2 Samuel|21:12-14|9}}).[[File:077.Jabesh-Gileadites_Recover_the_Bodies_of_Saul_and_His_Sons.jpg|thumb|Jabesh-Gileadites recover the bodies of Saul and his sons, Gustave Doré]]

==== House of Shallum ====
In the [[Books of Kings]] ({{Bibleverse|2 Kings|15:10|9}}, {{Bibleverse|2 Kings|15:13-14|9}}) [[Shallum of Israel]]'s father is identified as [[Jabesh]]. However, the passage may instead mention a [[toponym]], identifying that Shallum was "the son" of a city called Jabesh. In this view, Shallum may have originated from Jabesh-Gilead.<ref name="Freedman2">Freedman, Myers (2000), p. 664</ref>

=== Later years ===
In his ''[[Antiquities of the Jews]]'' (c. 93–94 CE), [[Josephus]] describes Jabesh Gilead as a metropolis in the Transjordan. In the early-4th century CE, Greek scholar [[Eusebius]] mentioned "Iabeis Galaad" in his ''[[Onomasticon (Eusebius)|Onomasticon]]'' as a "village beyond the Jordan located on the mountains six miles from the city of [[Pella, Jordan|Pella]] on the road to [[Jerash|Gerasa]]."<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=McDonald|first=Burton|url=https://www.bu.edu/asor/pubs/books-monographs/macdonald.pdf|title=East of the Jordan: Territories and Sites of the Hebrew Scriptures|publisher=American Schools of Oriental Research|year=2000|pages=202–203}}</ref>

==Identification==

The exact location of Jabesh-Gilead is debated. Most scholars identify it with [[Tell el-Maqlub]],<ref>{{Cite book|last=Merrill|first=S|title=East of the Jordan: a record of travel and observation in the countries of Moab, Gilead, and Bashan. R. Bentley|year=1883|location=New York: Scribner's|pages=440|orig-date=1881}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Noth|first=M.|date=1953|title=Jabesh-gilead: Ein Beitrag zur Methode alttestamentischer Topographie|journal=Zeitschrift des Deutschen Palästina-Vereins|pages=28–41}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Simons|first=J|title=The Geographical and Topographical Texts of the Old Testament: A Concise Commentary in XXXII Chapters|publisher=Brill|year=1959|location=Leiden|pages=315}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Aharoni|first=Y.|title=The Land of the Bible: A Historical Geography|publisher=Burns & Oates|year=1979|editor-last=Rainey|editor-first=A.F.|edition=2|location=London|pages=379, 437}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last1=Finkelstein|first1=Israel|title=Ugarit-Forschungen; Band 43 (2011)|last2=Lipschits|first2=Oded|last3=Koch|first3=Ido|year=2012|isbn=978-3-86835-086-9|location=[Erscheinungsort nicht ermittelbar]|pages=131|chapter=The Biblical Gilead: Observations on Identifications, Geographic Divisions and Territorial History.|oclc=1101929531}}</ref> but [[Tell Abu al-Kharaz]] is also frequently suggested.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Glueck|first=Nelson|date=February 1943|title=Jabesh-Gilead|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.2307/3218934|journal=Bulletin of the American Schools of Oriental Research|volume=89|issue=89 |pages=2–6|doi=10.2307/3218934|jstor=3218934 |s2cid=222428752 |issn=0003-097X|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Fischer|first1=Peter M.|last2=Herrmann|first2=Georgina|date=January 1995|title=A Carved Bone Object from Tell Abu al-Kharaz in Jordan: A Palestinian Workshop for Bone and Ivory?|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1179/lev.1995.27.1.145|journal=Levant|volume=27|issue=1|pages=145–163|doi=10.1179/lev.1995.27.1.145|issn=0075-8914|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Both sites were inhabited during the Iron Age and lie along [[Wadi Yabis|Wadi al-Yabis]], a stream believed to preserve the town's ancient name.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=McDonald|first=Burton|url=https://www.bu.edu/asor/pubs/books-monographs/macdonald.pdf|title=East of the Jordan: Territories and Sites of the Hebrew Scriptures|publisher=American Schools of Oriental Research|year=2000|pages=202–203}}</ref>
